chapter.title: Managing Your Money
chapter.description: Learn the real skills of personal finance: tracking income and expenses, budgeting with the 50/30/20 rule, building an emergency fund, and creating a spending plan that actually works for Indian teens.

data.content: Picture this. You get your pocket money — maybe 2,000 rupees, maybe 5,000. For about two days, you feel unstoppable. Then a Zomato order here, a movie plan there, some random Amazon impulse buy... and suddenly your UPI balance looks like a horror movie countdown.

data.text: Yaar, I got 3,000 rupees for my birthday last month. Genuinely no idea where it all went. Like, zero clue. Poof — gone.

data.content: That vanishing-money feeling? Totally normal. You're not bad with money — nobody ever showed you the two forces running your entire financial life. **Income** is money flowing in. **Expenses** is money flowing out. Everything in personal finance comes down to the gap between these two.

data.definition: Any money coming IN to you: pocket money, birthday gifts, freelance gigs, part-time tutoring, stipends. All of it counts.
Any money going OUT: food, transport, subscriptions, shopping, movie tickets — every single rupee that leaves your wallet or UPI app.

data.question: Priya earned Rs.3,000 from birthday gifts and spent it all without tracking. What two forces should she have been watching?

options.text: Savings and investments
Income (money in) and expenses (money out)
Loans and interest rates

data.alt: Two arrows showing money flowing in as income and money flowing out as expenses
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). Two bold arrows: a green-teal arrow pointing INTO a wallet labeled 'Income' (pocket money, gifts, part-time job icons nearby), and a red-coral arrow pointing OUT labeled 'Expenses' (food, phone, shopping bag icons). Clean, modern, fills the frame. No text except labels.

data.content: Here's where it gets interesting. There are two types of expenses, and mixing them up is where most people mess up their money. **Fixed expenses** stay the same every month — your phone recharge, that Netflix subscription, coaching class fees. You know the exact number before the month even starts.

data.definition: Costs that stay the same every month regardless of what you do. Phone plan, subscriptions, tuition fees, loan instalments.

data.question: Your Netflix subscription of Rs.199/month is an example of which type of expense?

options.text: Variable expense, because you can cancel it anytime
Fixed expense, because the amount stays the same every month
It is not an expense since it is entertainment

data.content: The average Indian teenager spends around 800 to 1,500 rupees a month on food delivery apps alone. That's up to 18,000 rupees a year quietly vanishing through Swiggy and Zomato — enough to buy a decent phone.

**Variable expenses** change every month depending on your choices. How many times you split a Zomato order with friends, whether you took an auto or walked, that impulse Flipkart buy at 2 AM. This is where your real control lives — you can't easily change your phone plan, but you 100% control how many bubble teas you order this week.

data.definition: Costs that change from month to month depending on your choices. Eating out, transport, shopping, entertainment — this is where you have the most control.

data.text: Bro, I tracked my spending for just one week. ONE. I was blowing 150 rupees a day on canteen snacks and chai. That's 4,500 a month — my entire pocket money raise from last year was going straight to samosas.

data.question: Which of the following is a variable expense?

options.text: Monthly phone recharge of Rs.299
Splitting a Zomato order with friends for Rs.350
Coaching class fees of Rs.2,000 per month

data.alt: Pie chart showing typical monthly expense breakdown for an Indian teen
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). A clean pie chart showing expense categories for an Indian teenager: Food & snacks (biggest slice), Transport (auto/metro), Phone recharge, Entertainment (movies/OTT), Shopping, and Savings. Each slice in a different shade of teal/mint. Bold, minimal, fills the space.

data.content: The formula is dead simple: **Income minus Expenses equals Surplus (or Deficit)**. Surplus means you have money left over — options, freedom, breathing room. Deficit means you spent more than you earned — and that's when stress kicks in.
Try this right now: open your UPI app and scroll through last week's transactions. Add them up. Most people are genuinely shocked when they see the real number. Awareness alone changes how you spend.

data.question: Arjun's pocket money is Rs.5,000 this month. He spent Rs.5,800 on food, transport, and shopping. What is his financial position?

options.text: Surplus of Rs.800
Deficit of Rs.800
Break-even
Surplus of Rs.5,800

data.alt: A simple equation showing Income minus Expenses equals Surplus or Deficit
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). Bold equation: Income (shown as stack of coins) MINUS Expenses (shown as shopping bags and food) EQUALS either a happy green surplus arrow pointing up or a red deficit arrow pointing down. Clean, bold shapes, no stick figures, fills the space.

data.content: Here's the thing nobody tells you: most people have a rough idea of how much they earn, but almost nobody has an accurate idea of how much they spend. Step one of managing money? Just know the actual numbers. That's it. That's the whole first step.

exercises.prompt: Sort these monthly expenses into Fixed vs. Variable
exercises.explanation: Fixed expenses are locked in — rent and loan payments don't care if you had a slow month. Variable expenses are in your control. That's exactly where your budgeting focus should go: reduce the variables, not stress about the fixed.

exercises.prompt: Arjun earns ₹32,000/month. His total expenses this month were ₹29,500. What's his financial position?

options.text: Deficit of ₹2,500
Surplus of ₹2,500
Surplus of ₹29,500
Break-even, neither surplus nor deficit

exercises.explanation: ₹32,000 − ₹29,500 = ₹2,500 surplus. That's his leftover money. Not bad, but also not a ton of cushion, which is why the next lessons matter.

exercises.scenario: Priya gets ₹25,000/month salary. Her fixed expenses: rent ₹8,000, phone loan instalment ₹1,200, insurance ₹500. Her variable expenses last month: groceries ₹3,500, eating out ₹4,200, transport ₹1,800, shopping ₹3,000, misc ₹1,500.
exercises.prompt: How much did Priya actually save this month?

options.text: ₹0, she spent everything
She went into deficit

exercises.explanation: Fixed: ₹8,000 + ₹1,200 + ₹500 = ₹9,700. Variable: ₹3,500 + ₹4,200 + ₹1,800 + ₹3,000 + ₹1,500 = ₹14,000. Total: ₹23,700. Surplus: ₹25,000 − ₹23,700 = ₹1,300. She saved something, but ₹4,200 on eating out (nearly 17% of income!) is worth a look.

exercises.prompt: Variable expenses are impossible to reduce because you need them to survive.
exercises.explanation: Variable expenses are literally the ones you have the most control over! Eating out vs. cooking, Ola vs. metro, branded shampoo vs. generic — these are all choices. Fixed expenses (rent, loan payments) are much harder to change quickly.

exercises.prompt: Which of these would count as income for a 21-year-old? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Monthly salary from internship
Cash gift from grandparents for Diwali
Selling old textbooks online
Money borrowed from a friend

exercises.explanation: Salary, gifts, and selling stuff all count as income, money genuinely coming in. But borrowed money is NOT income; it's a liability because you have to pay it back. Counting loans as income is how people accidentally think they're richer than they are.

data.content: Here's the problem with most money advice you'll hear from adults: it's either too vague ('just spend less, beta!') or insanely complicated (spreadsheets with 47 categories that nobody fills in after week two). What if there was one single rule that could handle your entire income?

data.text: Every uncle-aunty tells me to 'save more' but nobody actually explains HOW much. Like, is 100 rupees enough? 1,000? It's so frustratingly vague.

data.content: Fair question, Priya. There IS a simple answer. It's called the **50/30/20 Rule**, and it's survived since the early 2000s because it genuinely works. Every rupee you earn goes into one of three buckets. Needs: 50%. Wants: 30%. Savings: 20%. That's the whole thing.

data.definition: The actual money you receive after any deductions like taxes or PF. This is the number you budget with, not your gross salary.
A budgeting framework where 50% of your take-home income goes to Needs, 30% to Wants, and 20% to Savings or debt repayment.

data.question: In the 50/30/20 rule, what percentage goes to savings?

data.alt: Three buckets showing the 50/30/20 budget split with Indian examples
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). Three bold buckets in different teal shades. First bucket (darkest teal, 50%) labeled 'Needs' with icons: house, groceries, metro card. Second bucket (medium teal, 30%) labeled 'Wants' with icons: pizza, movie tickets, sneakers. Third bucket (lightest mint, 20%) labeled 'Savings' with icons: piggy bank, coins. Clean, bold shapes, fills the space.

data.content: Say you get 5,000 rupees pocket money a month. Here's the split: 2,500 for Needs (bus pass, phone recharge, school supplies). 1,500 for Wants (splitting Zomato orders, movies, that thing you've been eyeing on Amazon). 1,000 straight to Savings. Simple math, powerful habit.

The 50/30/20 rule was popularized by Elizabeth Warren (before she became a US Senator) in her book 'All Your Worth.' It was designed to be so simple that literally anyone could follow it without a finance degree or a spreadsheet addiction.

data.question: You get Rs.8,000 pocket money this month. According to the 50/30/20 rule, how much can you spend on Wants (movies, eating out, shopping)?

options.text: Rs.8,000 — it is all pocket money so it is all wants

data.content: **Needs** are the non-negotiables — things you genuinely cannot function without. For you, that might be metro/bus fare to school, phone recharge, basic meals, and study materials. For someone earning a salary in Bangalore, it's rent, groceries (home-cooked, not restaurant), electricity, and transport.

data.text: Here's where people mess up every single time: eating out is a WANT, not a need. You need food, haan. But you don't need butter chicken from Zomato at surge pricing. Dal-chawal at home is a need. Restaurant food is a want. Simple.

data.content: **Wants** are the things that make life fun but aren't survival. Eating out with your squad, Netflix, new clothes, that 500-rupee Starbucks coffee you keep posting on Instagram. The 30% bucket says you absolutely get to enjoy life — just within a number.

data.question: You order butter chicken from Zomato for Rs.350. Which 50/30/20 bucket does this fall into?

options.text: Needs, because food is a basic necessity
Wants, because restaurant or delivery food is a lifestyle choice
Savings, because you saved time by not cooking

data.content: Most young people have the Wants and Savings buckets completely backwards. They blow 30% on fun and 'try to save' the 20% from whatever's left. Spoiler: the saving rarely happens. Flip the script. Save first, then enjoy the rest guilt-free.

data.definition: The habit of transferring money to savings BEFORE spending on anything else. Treat savings like a bill that's due on day one of every month.

data.content: **Savings** is your 20%. And here's the mindset shift that changes everything: savings isn't what's left over after you spend. It's what you set aside FIRST. The day your pocket money or income arrives, move that 20% somewhere you won't touch it. Even 500 rupees a month. Future you will literally thank present you.

data.alt: Example 50/30/20 split applied to 5000 rupees pocket money
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). A 5000 rupee note at the top, with three arrows splitting down to three labeled sections: Needs 2500 (bus pass, phone icon), Wants 1500 (pizza, headphones icon), Savings 1000 (piggy bank icon). Bold, clean shapes, minimal text, fills the space.

options.text: Spend on your wants before paying any bills
Transfer money to savings before spending on anything else
Pay off all your debts before saving anything
Only spend money on yourself, never on others

data.content: Real talk though: this rule is a **guide, not a law**. If your Diwali shopping month doesn't fit 50/30/20 perfectly, that's fine. Even 60/25/15 or 70/20/10 is infinitely better than having zero plan. The real goal is giving every rupee a purpose so money doesn't just vanish.

If the numbers feel tight, start with the Savings bucket first. Even 500 rupees a month builds the habit. You can scale it up as your income grows. The consistency matters way more than the percentage.

data.alt: Visual comparing someone with a budget plan versus without one
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). Split panel: LEFT shows a calm person with organized money buckets, wallet still has cash at month end, labeled 'With a plan'. RIGHT shows a stressed person with money flying away in all directions, empty wallet, labeled 'Without a plan'. Bold flat shapes, expressive but no stick figures, fills the space.

exercises.title: 50/30/20 Budget Calculator
exercises.formula: { needs: salary * 0.50, wants: salary * 0.30, savings: salary * 0.20 }

followUpQuestion.prompt: On a salary of ₹30,000, how much should ideally go toward 'Wants' per month?
followUpQuestion.explanation: 30% of ₹30,000 = ₹9,000 for Wants. That's ₹300/day on average for eating out, entertainment, shopping, fun. Not nothing, but definitely a real number that keeps you on track.

exercises.scenario: Meera earns ₹26,000/month. Her expenses: rent ₹8,500, groceries ₹3,200, auto/metro ₹1,800, phone bill ₹349, eating out ₹3,800, OTT subscriptions ₹498, gym ₹999, new kurtas she bought online ₹2,400, savings transferred ₹3,000.
exercises.prompt: Which 50/30/20 bucket is Meera most over-budget in?

options.text: Needs, her fixed costs are too high
Wants, she's spending more than 30% on lifestyle
Savings, she's not saving enough compared to the 20% target
She's perfectly balanced

exercises.explanation: Meera's Needs (rent + groceries + transport + phone): ₹13,849, that's 53% of income, slightly over but close. Her Wants (eating out + OTTs + gym + clothes): ₹7,697, that's about 30%, right on target. Her Savings: ₹3,000, that's only 11.5%, well under the 20% target of ₹5,200. To fix this, she'd need to trim her Needs or Wants to free up another ₹2,200 for savings.

exercises.prompt: Sort these expenses into the correct 50/30/20 bucket

items.text: Monthly SIP (auto-investing in a mutual fund)

exercises.explanation: Needs = survival basics. Wants = quality of life. Savings = future you. The tricky ones: a basic phone plan is a Need; eating out is always a Want; auto-investments (like SIPs in mutual funds) and emergency fund contributions both count as Savings.

exercises.prompt: The 50/30/20 rule means you must save exactly 20% of your income, anything less is a failure.
exercises.explanation: The 50/30/20 rule is a framework, not a test to pass or fail. If you're saving 10% consistently and building the habit, that's better than saving 0% while stressing about perfection. Adjust the percentages to your real life, just always have a number for savings.

exercises.prompt: Rahul's phone dies and he needs to buy a replacement to work (he's a delivery driver). He buys a basic smartphone on monthly instalments, ₹1,500/month. Which budget bucket does this instalment belong in?

options.text: Wants (30%), it's a phone, which is a luxury
Needs (50%), it's required for his income
Savings (20%), buying assets is like saving
It doesn't fit any bucket and should be avoided

exercises.explanation: Since Rahul's livelihood literally depends on having a working phone, this is a Need. If he were upgrading from a working phone to a fancier model, it'd be a Want. Context matters, it's not the item, it's the function it serves.

lessons.title: Emergency Funds - Why You Need One

data.content: Imagine you're cruising along, managing your money, feeling good about life. Then your phone screen cracks — repair: 4,000 rupees. Then a family member gets sick and you need to rush home — train ticket: 2,500 rupees. Both in the same month. Where does that money come from?

data.text: Last month my laptop charger died right before exams. 2,800 rupees for a replacement. I had to borrow from THREE different friends. It was so awkward, never again.

data.content: Here's the truth: unexpected expenses aren't actually that unexpected. They happen to everyone, every few months, like clockwork. The question isn't IF something will cost you money out of nowhere. The question is: when it happens, do you have a safety net ready?

data.definition: A separate stash of money set aside ONLY for genuine emergencies: medical issues, urgent travel, broken essentials. Not for sales, not for fun, not for 'but it was on discount.'

data.question: Priya had to borrow from three friends to replace her laptop charger. What could have prevented this?

options.text: A credit card with a high limit
An emergency fund set aside for unexpected costs
Buying a cheaper laptop that does not need a charger

data.alt: An umbrella protecting money from unexpected expenses raining down
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). A large teal umbrella shielding a stack of coins and rupee notes. Above the umbrella, rain drops shaped like common emergencies: a cracked phone, a medical cross, a broken bike, a train ticket. Below the umbrella, the money is safe and dry. Bold flat shapes, fills the space.

data.content: So what counts as a real emergency? Medical costs, urgent family travel, a broken phone or laptop you actually need for school. What does NOT count: a Myntra sale, a concert you forgot to budget for, or running out of money because you over-ordered on Swiggy. Those are planning problems, not emergencies.

Think of your emergency fund as the wall between you and debt. Even as a teenager, having 5,000 to 10,000 rupees stashed away means you never have to do the embarrassing 'yaar, can you lend me...' phone call. That wall is priceless.

data.question: A big Myntra sale is happening with 50% off sneakers. Is this a valid reason to dip into your emergency fund?

options.text: Yes, 50% off is too good to miss
No, a sale is a want, not a genuine emergency
Yes, if the sneakers will eventually become a need

data.content: How much should you save? The adult rule is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses. But as a teenager, even 5,000 to 15,000 rupees gives you a real safety net. Start with 500 rupees a month. In 10 months, you've built a 5,000-rupee emergency fund. That's enough to handle most surprises without borrowing.

data.text: I started putting aside just 300 rupees every month in a separate UPI account. After 8 months, my cycle needed repairs — 2,400 rupees. I just paid for it. No stress, no borrowing. Best feeling ever.

data.alt: A progress bar showing emergency fund building up month by month
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). A horizontal progress bar filling up over 10 months, starting from 0 and reaching 5000 rupees. Each month's addition of 500 is marked. A small flag at the 5000 target. Below, three icons showing what the fund can cover: phone repair, medical visit, emergency travel. Bold, clean, fills the space.

data.question: Arjun saved Rs.300 per month for 8 months. How much did he have in his emergency fund?

data.content: The golden rule: keep this money **separate** from your spending account. If it sits in the same place you use for Paytm and Zomato, you WILL spend it. Open a different savings account, use a separate UPI ID, or even keep cash in an envelope at home. Out of sight, out of temptation.

A single hospital visit for something like a fracture or appendicitis can cost 50,000 to 1,50,000 rupees in India, even at a decent hospital. Health insurance helps, but having emergency cash means you're never stuck waiting for claim approvals while you're in pain.

data.question: Why should your emergency fund be kept separate from your regular spending account?

options.text: Banks give higher interest on separate accounts
If it is in the same account you use for daily spending, you will likely spend it
It is illegal to keep emergency savings in a spending account

data.content: Here's what your emergency fund really protects you from: **debt**. Without one, every surprise expense becomes borrowed money — from friends, from family, or worse, from those sketchy instant loan apps that charge insane interest. Your emergency fund is the difference between 'handled it' and 'owe people money.'

data.definition: Money that's easy and quick to access with no penalties or waiting period. Your emergency fund needs to be liquid — not locked in a fixed deposit you can't touch for 3 years.

data.alt: Two paths: one person with an emergency fund stays calm, another without one panics
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). Split panel showing two scenarios after a phone breaks. LEFT: person with emergency fund calmly pays, life continues normally. RIGHT: person without fund panics, borrows from friends, stress symbols everywhere. Bold flat shapes, expressive faces but no stick figures, fills the space.

data.content: Start today. Not tomorrow, not Monday — today. Transfer 200 or 500 rupees to a separate spot. The amount barely matters. Starting the habit is everything. You can always increase it later.

followUpQuestion.prompt: If your monthly essential expenses are ₹18,000 and you want 3 months of coverage, what's your emergency fund target?
followUpQuestion.explanation: ₹18,000 x 3 months = ₹54,000. That's your 3-month target. A 6-month target would be ₹1,08,000. Start with 3 months, it's a real milestone that's achievable in under 2 years at ₹3,000/month.

exercises.scenario: Vikram has ₹20,000 in savings. He's been thinking of investing it in a mutual fund. Then his motorbike's engine needs replacement, ₹14,000. He has no emergency fund. His options: take it from savings, use a credit card, or borrow from family.
exercises.prompt: What does this situation illustrate?

options.text: Vikram shouldn't have bought a motorbike
Unexpected expenses happen, a dedicated emergency fund prevents them from derailing your finances
Savings accounts are better than mutual funds
Vikram should have spent less on food to save more

exercises.explanation: Vikram's savings are now at ₹6,000, barely anything left. If he'd had an emergency fund of ₹45,000 separate from his investing money, he'd cover the repair without touching his investment. The emergency fund and investment fund are two different pots for two different purposes.

exercises.prompt: Which of these qualify as genuine emergencies that an emergency fund should be used for? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Unexpected hospitalization for ₹40,000
iPhone 16 launch sale, 20% off this weekend only
Job loss, 2 months of rent while job-hunting
Rent cheque bounced because you forgot to transfer
Flight home for a family medical crisis

exercises.explanation: Real emergencies are unplanned, urgent, and genuinely necessary, health, job loss, family crisis. A sale is not an emergency (it's a want with a deadline, the classic trap). Bouncing rent because of a planning error is a budget problem, not an emergency. Your fund is precious, guard it.

exercises.prompt: Where is the BEST place to keep your emergency fund?

options.text: Under your mattress (cash, always accessible)
A high-interest savings account or liquid mutual fund
A 3-year fixed deposit for maximum interest
Invested in the stock market for better returns

exercises.explanation: Emergency funds need to be accessible quickly (within 1-2 days) AND earn some interest. A high-interest savings account (6-7% at small finance banks) or liquid mutual fund hits both. Cash earns nothing and can be stolen. A long FD locks your money and charges a penalty for early withdrawal. Stocks can be down 30% exactly when you need the money.

exercises.prompt: If you have a credit card with a high limit, you don't need an emergency fund.
exercises.explanation: A credit card is debt, not savings. Using it for emergencies means you pay 36-48% annual interest on top of the emergency cost, a ₹40,000 medical bill becomes ₹53,000+ if you take 9 months to pay it off. An emergency fund costs you nothing. A credit card costs you plenty.

data.content: Budgets have a massive image problem. You hear 'budget' and picture some sad spreadsheet that sucks all joy out of life. But here's what a budget actually is: a **plan for your money**. Instead of wondering where it all went at month-end, you decide where it goes at the start.

data.text: Budgeting sounds like something my parents would force me to do. Like writing a diary — nobody actually keeps it up past a week, let's be real.

data.content: Okay fair, but think about it this way. When you're planning your Diwali shopping, you already do a version of budgeting — you figure out how much you can spend on crackers, on gifts, on new clothes, and you make it fit. A monthly budget is the exact same thing, just for your whole life.

One mindset flip that changes everything: a budget doesn't restrict your spending. It ALLOWS you to spend guilt-free because you planned for it. If your budget says 1,500 for eating out, spending 1,200 at a restaurant feels great. Without a budget, the same 1,200 feels suspicious and stressful.

data.question: What is the best way to think about a budget?

options.text: A punishment that stops you from having fun
A plan for your money that you set at the start of the month
A diary of regrets about past spending

data.alt: A phone screen showing a simple budget app with categories and amounts
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). A smartphone screen showing a clean budget app interface. Categories listed: Needs (rent, food, transport), Wants (eating out, entertainment), Savings. Each has a teal progress bar showing spent vs. budgeted. Total at bottom shows 'Left to spend: 2,953'. Bold, modern app design, fills the space.

data.content: The simplest way to budget: list your income at the top, then list every expense below it. Make sure the total expenses are less than the income. Sounds obvious, right? But most people have literally never written it all down in one place.

A smarter approach is **Zero-Based Budgeting**. Every rupee you earn gets assigned a job. 1,200 goes to transport. 1,500 goes to food. 1,000 goes to savings. Income minus all assignments equals zero. You haven't spent it all — you've *planned* it all. Nothing is floating around unaccounted for.

data.definition: A method where every rupee of income is assigned a specific purpose until Income minus All Allocations equals 0. Nothing is 'leftover' and nothing is unplanned.

data.text: I just use a notes app on my phone. Every 1st, I write down my pocket money and assign every rupee. Takes 10 minutes max. And bro, I've saved more in 3 months than I did the entire previous year. It's wild.

data.question: In zero-based budgeting, what should Income minus All Allocations equal?

options.text: A large positive number so you have leftover money
Zero, because every rupee is assigned a specific purpose
A negative number so you know you are spending wisely

data.alt: A zero-based budget example for a student with 5000 rupees
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). A clean budget template showing: Income 5000 at top. Below: Transport 1200, Phone recharge 299, Food/snacks 1500, Entertainment 800, Clothes 500, Savings 701. Total allocations: 5000. Remaining: 0. Checkmark next to zero. Teal color scheme, bold flat design, fills the space.

data.content: What about when your income isn't regular? Maybe you earn different amounts from tutoring or freelance work each month. The trick: budget based on your **lowest expected month**. If you earn between 3,000 and 8,000, budget for 3,000. Anything extra is a bonus you split between savings and fun.

data.question: If your tutoring income varies between Rs.4,000 and Rs.10,000 per month, what amount should you base your budget on?

options.text: Rs.10,000, the maximum you could earn
Rs.7,000, the average of the two
Rs.4,000, the lowest expected income

data.content: You WILL mess up your budget sometimes. Everyone does. A budget isn't a promise to be perfect — it's a system to catch yourself when you drift. Missing one month and getting back on track? Totally normal. Missing every month and never checking? That's the real problem.

Three ways to track your spending right now: check your **PhonePe/Paytm** transaction history (it's already tracking every UPI payment), use a simple notes app where you log each expense the same day, or try apps like **Money Manager** or **Walnut** that auto-categorize. Low-tech works just as well as high-tech.

data.definition: Recording every purchase you make — UPI, cash, or card — so you can see exactly where your money actually went versus where you planned for it to go.

data.content: Research shows that people who simply write down their expenses end up spending 15-20% less without any other effort. Your brain automatically thinks twice before ordering that third Zomato meal when you've already logged the first two.

data.alt: A calendar showing a monthly money review date circled
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). A calendar page with the last Sunday circled in teal and labeled 'Money Date'. Around it: icons of a phone showing transactions, a checklist, a small piggy bank with a checkmark. Mood is calm and organized, not stressful. Bold flat shapes, fills the space.

data.content: Pro tip: schedule a **monthly money check-in** with yourself. Just 15 minutes on the last Sunday of each month. Look at what you spent. Did you hit your savings goal? Which category blew up? Any subscriptions you forgot about? This is where you catch small leaks before they become floods.

data.definition: When your spending automatically rises to match every increase in income, leaving you no better off despite earning more. The sneaky enemy of actually building wealth.

data.question: Priya's pocket money increased from Rs.3,000 to Rs.5,000. She immediately started ordering more food, buying more clothes, and going out more — now she saves the same Rs.0 as before. What is this called?

options.text: Smart spending, because she is enjoying her extra income
Lifestyle creep, because her spending rose to match her income increase
Inflation, because everything costs more now
Budgeting, because she is spending her full income

data.content: When you get more pocket money or a raise someday, resist the urge to upgrade everything immediately. Keep spending roughly the same and route the extra to savings. This one habit is literally how people with modest incomes build real wealth over time.

exercises.scenario: Aditya earns ₹22,000/month from his first job. He sits down on the 1st of the month and writes out his plan: Rent ₹7,500, Groceries ₹3,000, Transport ₹1,200, Phone ₹299, Eating out ₹2,000, Entertainment ₹800, Clothes ₹1,201, Emergency fund ₹3,000, Savings ₹3,000. Every rupee has a job. He then tracks every expense during the month to make sure he sticks to the plan.
exercises.prompt: Which budgeting method is Aditya using?

options.text: Zero-based budgeting
The 50/30/20 rule with no tracking
Spending whatever feels right each month

exercises.explanation: Aditya assigned every rupee of his ₹22,000 a specific purpose: ₹7,500 + ₹3,000 + ₹1,200 + ₹299 + ₹2,000 + ₹800 + ₹1,201 + ₹3,000 + ₹3,000 = ₹22,000. Income minus all allocations equals zero. Nothing is unplanned, nothing is 'floating'. That's zero-based budgeting.

exercises.prompt: Priya's income varies between ₹10,000 and ₹18,000 per month doing freelance design work. When building her monthly budget, she should base it on:

options.text: ₹18,000, the maximum she could earn
₹14,000, her average monthly income
₹10,000, her minimum reliable income
₹0, freelance income can't be budgeted

exercises.explanation: When income varies, always budget for the floor, your lowest reliable amount. If she budgets for ₹18,000 and earns ₹10,000 one month, she's in deficit. If she budgets for ₹10,000 and earns ₹18,000, she has ₹8,000 extra to split between savings and fun. The conservative approach always wins.

exercises.prompt: Rajan gets a ₹5,000 raise (now ₹35,000/month). Sort these responses to his new income into Smart Move vs. Lifestyle Creep

items.text: Increase monthly savings or investments by ₹2,000/month
Move from shared flat to solo apartment (+₹5,000 rent)
Upgrade eating out budget from ₹2,000 to ₹5,000/month
Keep expenses the same, put ₹5,000 into emergency fund faster
Add a small ₹1,000 'fun' increase and save the rest
Subscribe to every OTT platform now that he 'can afford it'

exercises.explanation: A raise is an opportunity. Lifestyle creep means your expenses grow as fast as your income, leaving you no richer in real terms. Smart moves direct most of the new income toward financial goals, with a small enjoyment bump. You can absolutely enjoy more as you earn more, just not ALL of it, immediately.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are good habits for sticking to a monthly budget? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Tracking every UPI and cash expense
Reviewing your budget once a month
Deleting your banking app so you don't see the balance
Setting up an automatic transfer to savings on salary day
Building a slightly flexible 'miscellaneous' buffer

exercises.explanation: Tracking, reviewing, and automating are the three pillars of budget consistency. A misc buffer (₹500-₹1,000) handles the small surprises without blowing your plan. Ignoring your balance is the opposite of budgeting, out of sight doesn't mean out of debt.

exercises.prompt: A budget fails if you spend even ₹1 more than planned in any category.
exercises.explanation: A budget is a living plan, not a rigid contract. Going ₹200 over on groceries and ₹300 under on transport is perfectly fine, the overall balance is what matters. The goal is awareness and direction, not military precision. Flexibility is what makes a budget sustainable long-term.

data.content: Alright, you've got the theory down. You know the 50/30/20 split. You know what an emergency fund is. You know what budgeting actually means. Now comes the real test: living it out, decision by decision.

data.text: Wait, we get to actually simulate a whole month? Like making real decisions about rent and food and everything? This is SO much better than just reading about it.

data.content: The Month One simulator puts you in someone's shoes on their first real job. 30,000 rupees salary. One month in Bangalore. Real decisions at every turn. Rent is due. A friend's birthday pops up. A medical thing hits out of nowhere. You'll make choices and see immediately what they do to your wallet.

data.question: In the Month One simulator, what is the salary you start with?

data.alt: Preview of the Month One simulator showing a wallet with 30,000 rupees and a Bangalore apartment

Next to it, a simple illustrated Bangalore scene with apartment building, auto-rickshaw, and chai stall. Mood is exciting and slightly challenging. Bold flat shapes, fills the space.

data.content: Fair warning: there's no perfect run on this simulator. There are smart decisions and expensive ones, but no path where everything works out magically. The point is feeling the trade-offs before real life throws them at you. Ready?

Before you start, remember three things. **Needs come first**: pay rent, buy groceries, keep the lights on. **Emergency fund before fun**: seriously, you just learned why. And most importantly: **small daily decisions add up way more than you think**.

data.definition: When choosing one option means giving up another. Every rupee you spend on one thing is a rupee you can't spend or save elsewhere. The simulator is all about feeling these trade-offs in real time.

data.question: If you take a Rs.150 auto instead of a Rs.25 metro ride every working day for a month (24 days), how much extra do you spend?

data.text: I tried to end the month with 6,000 saved. Tight, but totally doable if you cook at home and skip one or two splurges. Think of it like a game — the savings number is your score.

data.alt: A badge showing Budget Boss achievement for saving 20% in Month One
data.prompt: Flat illustration with teal color palette (#1ABC9C). A circular badge/medal design with 'Budget Boss' text and a trophy icon in the center. Around the edge: '20% Savings Target'. Teal and gold colors. Bold, celebratory but clean design. Fills the space.

data.content: Badge target: End the month with Rs.6,000 or more saved (that's 20% of Rs.30,000). That earns you the 'Budget Boss' badge. Totally achievable — but it requires real choices at every step.

You'll face decisions about cooking vs. ordering in, cheap transport vs. comfortable transport, saying yes to friends vs. protecting your budget. No single right answer for any of them. But by the end, you'll have a gut feel for what actually matters and what's just noise.

data.question: What is a trade-off in the context of money decisions?

options.text: Trading stocks on the share market
Choosing one option means giving up another because every rupee can only be spent once
Exchanging old rupee notes for new ones at a bank

One path leads to a happy ending with savings (teal, bright), another leads to a tight ending with barely anything left (dimmer). Shows key decision moments: rent, groceries, birthday dinner, emergency. Bold flat shapes, fills the space.

data.content: Studies show that people who practice financial decisions in simulations make 23% better money choices in real life. Your brain learns from simulated stress the same way it learns from real stress — minus the actual consequences. Free practice, real results.

Remember: every choice here — cooking vs. ordering food, saying yes or no to a trip — mirrors the exact decisions you'll face when you start earning for real. The stakes right now are zero. The learning is 100% real. Let's go.

exercises.prompt: You start the Month One simulator with ₹30,000. What should be your FIRST financial action?

options.text: Go out and celebrate your first salary!
Pay rent and set aside emergency fund contribution
Check what's on sale online
Invest everything in the stock market

exercises.explanation: Needs (like rent) and savings transfers come first, before any discretionary spending. Paying rent and contributing to your emergency fund on day one means the 'important money' is safe no matter what happens during the rest of the month.

exercises.prompt: Saving ₹6,000 from a ₹30,000 salary in Month One (your very first month) is unrealistic and too hard.
exercises.explanation: ₹6,000 from ₹30,000 is exactly 20%, the savings target of the 50/30/20 rule. With ₹15,000 for needs, ₹9,000 for wants, and ₹6,000 saved, the math works. It's tight (especially for Bangalore), but it's doable, especially if you cook, use public transport, and skip one or two splurges. That's the point of the simulator.

simulation.title: Month One
simulation.description: You just got your first real job offer, junior analyst at a Bangalore tech startup. Salary: ₹30,000/month. You've moved into a shared flat with a college friend. This is it. Month One starts now.
simulation.badgeDescription: Saved ₹6,000 or more in Month One, hit the 20% savings target on the first try.

nodes.narrative: Day 1. Salary just hit: ₹30,000. It's sitting in your account, glowing on the screen. Your flatmate Rohan is already texting: 'Dude first salary! There's this new place in Koramangala, ₹1,500 a head minimum. We're going.' Meanwhile, your rent of ₹9,500 is due in 3 days.

choices.text: Pay rent immediately AND transfer ₹3,000 to emergency fund savings
choices.feedback: Chip gives you a solid nod. 'Needs and savings locked on day one. You've got ₹17,500 to work with for the month. Strong start, very strong.'

choices.text: Go out with Rohan tonight (₹1,500), pay rent later this week
choices.feedback: Chip raises an eyebrow. 'First salary, first night out. Classic move. Just don't forget — rent is coming in 3 days and it doesn't care about your Koramangala memories.'

choices.text: Pay rent immediately, skip the emergency fund for now
choices.feedback: Chip sighs gently. 'Rent paid — good instinct. But skipping the emergency fund is a gamble. Something ALWAYS comes up. Mark my words.'

nodes.narrative: Rent and emergency fund: sorted. You have ₹17,500 left. It's Day 3 and your kitchen is completely empty — not even chai patti. Option: stock up properly with a big grocery run, or just keep ordering food until you feel settled in.

choices.text: Big grocery run — rice, dal, veggies, eggs, the works (₹2,500)
choices.feedback: Chip approves. 'Kitchen stocked for two weeks. Every meal you cook saves ₹100-₹200 versus Swiggy. Over a month, that's serious money.'

choices.text: Just eat out this week, do groceries later (₹4,000 this week on food)
choices.feedback: Chip grimaces. '₹4,000 on food in one week. Not catastrophic, but this month just got noticeably tighter. Hope you like cooking in Week 2.'

choices.text: Split the difference — small grocery run (₹1,200) plus a few cheap meals out (₹1,000)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Balanced approach. You've got basics at home and didn't blow the food budget. Practical.'

nodes.narrative: Fun night out — dinner plus drinks with Rohan = ₹1,500. Great memories. You wake up to a rent reminder notification. Pay it: ₹9,500 gone. You're at ₹19,000 now. Kitchen still completely empty — Week 1 groceries needed.

choices.text: Do a proper grocery run (₹2,500) and commit to cooking this week
choices.feedback: Chip nods. 'Late start but you're course-correcting. Kitchen stocked. Smart recovery.'

choices.text: Keep eating out for now, settle into a routine before cooking (₹4,000 for the week)
choices.feedback: Chip does the math quietly. 'Between the night out and eating all week, you've spent ₹14,000 in 4 days. Just 12 days left. Yikes.'

choices.text: Quick grocery basics (₹1,500) and ask Rohan to cook together this week to save money
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Teamwork budget hack! Cooking together splits the effort and the cost. Rohan might even be a decent chef. Win-win.'

nodes.narrative: Rent paid, ₹20,500 remaining but no emergency fund. Your phone is running slow and you keep seeing ads for a mid-range phone (₹12,999 on Flipkart, ₹1,083/month on EMI). Your current phone works, it's just frustrating.

choices.text: Do a grocery run (₹2,500), ignore the phone ad completely
choices.feedback: Chip smiles. 'Phone works. Food is essential. You just picked needs over wants. Correct priorities.'

choices.text: Buy the phone on EMI (₹1,083/month starts now) plus groceries (₹2,500)
choices.feedback: Chip squints. 'New phone when the old one still works, no emergency fund, and now you've added a monthly EMI. That's a want dressed up as a need. Just saying.'

choices.text: Groceries (₹2,500) and set up emergency fund with ₹2,000 (better late than never)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Ah, the guilt kicked in! But seriously, good call. Even ₹2,000 in an emergency fund is better than zero. Better late than never is actually great financial wisdom.'

nodes.narrative: Kitchen is stocked, Week 2 arrives. Your college friend Tanya's birthday is Saturday. She's planned dinner at a fancy place in Indiranagar — your share will be ₹1,200 to ₹1,500. You also haven't transferred anything extra to savings this month.

choices.text: Go to the dinner (₹1,200), you can save a bit less this month
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Friendship is real and it matters. Just know the month is tighter now. Worth it? Probably. Plan for it next time.'

choices.text: Skip the dinner, send a heartfelt message plus a small online gift (₹300)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Bold call. Some friends totally get it. Some might feel hurt. But your budget just thanked you. ₹900 saved.'

choices.text: Go but suggest a cheaper restaurant to the group first (settle on ₹600)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'The negotiation move. Socially a little risky, financially brilliant. Respect for speaking up.'

nodes.narrative: Food's been expensive but you're surviving. Week 2 hits with a double whammy: Tanya's birthday dinner (₹1,200 your share), AND your office announces a formal dress-code event next week. You don't own formal clothes. Cheapest option: basic shirt and trousers from a local store (₹2,500). Premium outfit for 'first impression': ₹5,500.

choices.text: Skip Tanya's dinner, buy the basic office outfit (₹2,500)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Work comes first — your career is your income source. Tanya will understand. Wise priorities.'

choices.text: Go to dinner AND buy the premium outfit (₹1,200 + ₹5,500 = ₹6,700)
choices.feedback: Chip is calculating frantically. 'You're draining fast. This month is going to be extremely tight from here. Hope nothing unexpected happens... (it will).'

choices.text: Buy the basic outfit, attend dinner but cap your share at ₹600 (order light)
choices.feedback: Chip exhales. 'Compromise. Work need covered, friendship partially covered, budget damaged but not destroyed. Decent damage control.'

nodes.narrative: New phone on EMI plus groceries — sorted. Week 2 arrives. Your manager asks the team to subscribe to a paid collaboration tool (₹850/month, company will reimburse in 60 days — but you pay upfront). AND Tanya's birthday dinner is Saturday (₹1,200 share).

choices.text: Pay for both — work tool ₹850 and birthday dinner ₹1,200
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Work need covered, friendship covered. But with a phone EMI already running, every rupee matters now. Tread carefully from here.'

choices.text: Pay work tool only, skip dinner and send Tanya a message (₹850)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Work reimbursement coming eventually. Social life on hold for now. Practical and painful — welcome to adulting.'

choices.text: Pay work tool, attend dinner but keep it cheap — order just one item (₹400)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'You showed up, you kept it light, and the work expense is handled. Middle path executed well.'

nodes.narrative: Week 3. The unexpected thing happens (it always does). You wake up with food poisoning — bad street food yesterday. Doctor visit: ₹500 consultation. Medicines: ₹800. Total health cost: ₹1,300. This is exactly the kind of thing an emergency fund is for.

choices.text: Pay from your remaining money (₹1,300 from wallet)
choices.feedback: Chip looks thoughtful. 'Handled it. But notice: that ₹1,300 was supposed to be savings or fun money. This is literally why emergency funds exist. Lesson learned?'

choices.text: Ask Rohan to lend you ₹1,300 (you'll pay back next month)
choices.feedback: Chip winces. 'Month One and already borrowing from your flatmate. Rohan is cool about it, but this is a habit you really don't want to start.'

choices.text: Visit the government hospital (free consultation) and buy generic medicines from Jan Aushadhi (₹350 total)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Government hospital plus generic medicines. Same treatment, fraction of the cost. You just saved ₹950. This is the kind of awareness that builds wealth over time.'

nodes.narrative: Tanya was a bit quiet about you skipping, but she understood. Week 3: food poisoning hits (bad street food). Doctor ₹500 plus medicines ₹800 = ₹1,300. Since you kept earlier costs low, this stings less — but it's still unplanned.

choices.text: Pay the ₹1,300 from your budget — you can absorb it
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Handled. You're lower than ideal but still in positive territory because you kept earlier costs down. That restraint is paying off right now.'

choices.text: Visit the government hospital (free) and buy generic medicines from Jan Aushadhi store (₹400 total)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Smart move. Government hospitals and generic medicine stores save serious money. Same treatment, fraction of the cost. ₹900 saved that stays in your wallet.'

choices.text: Borrow ₹1,300 from Rohan and pay him back later
choices.feedback: Chip: 'You have the money to cover this, but you're choosing to borrow anyway. That's a red flag. When you can afford it, pay your own way.'

nodes.narrative: Good middle ground on the dinner. Week 3 brings an unexpected surprise: your laptop charger dies (and you work from home some days). Branded replacement: ₹2,800. Compatible third-party charger (same wattage, reliable brand): ₹950.

choices.text: Buy the branded charger (₹2,800) — work tools should be quality
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Quality argument is valid. But ₹2,800 when you're already stretched? That's premium pricing for peace of mind you might not need.'

choices.text: Buy the third-party charger (₹950) — same function, lower cost
choices.feedback: Chip nods. 'Same voltage, same outcome. ₹1,850 saved. That's basically a full emergency fund contribution right there.'

choices.text: Ask your office if they can provide a charger since you work from home (₹0 if they say yes)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Now THAT is financial thinking. Asking costs nothing. Worst case they say no and you buy the third-party one. Best case: free charger. Always ask.'

nodes.narrative: Work event handled. Tanya situation managed. Week 3: your work-from-home setup needs a chair (you've been sitting on the floor — your back is staging a revolt). Options: decent IKEA chair (₹3,500), second-hand one from OLX (₹500), or just tolerate it for 2 more weeks.

choices.text: Buy the IKEA chair (₹3,500) — you'll use it every single day
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Long-term thinking, but expensive timing. Your back says thank you. Your budget says please don't do this again this month.'

choices.text: Buy the second-hand OLX chair (₹500) — functional is all you need right now
choices.feedback: Chip applauds. 'OLX is massively underrated. ₹500 for something that works perfectly fine? Budget win of the month.'

choices.text: Survive 2 more weeks on the floor, handle it in Month 2 budget
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Commitment to the budget is admirable. Your spine might file a complaint, but your wallet is throwing a party.'

nodes.narrative: You're stretched thin after the dinner and premium outfit. Week 3: Rohan suggests a weekend trip to Nandi Hills with friends (₹1,800 for petrol plus food). It sounds amazing. But your wallet is looking worryingly pale.

choices.text: Go on the trip (₹1,800) — you really need the break
choices.feedback: Chip covers his face. 'You're now dangerously low. Even a small unexpected expense — a doctor visit, a phone repair — could push you into deficit territory.'

choices.text: Skip the trip, be honest with Rohan about being tight on money
choices.feedback: Chip breathes out slowly. 'Good call. Real friends understand money struggles, especially in Month One. This decision might be what saves the entire month.'

choices.text: Suggest a cheaper alternative — chai and sunset at Cubbon Park (₹200 total)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Creative substitution! You still hung out, still made memories, but spent ₹1,600 less. This is what budget-smart social life looks like.'

nodes.narrative: Work tool and birthday handled. Week 3: partial reimbursement arrives — ₹750 instead of ₹850 (receipt format issue). ₹100 lost to paperwork. Meanwhile, grocery supplies are running low.

choices.text: Restock groceries properly (₹1,800 for the next 10 days)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Reimbursement partially covered groceries. Cooking at home is the right call here. Keep it going.'

choices.text: Just order food delivery this week, deal with groceries next month (₹3,000)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'You're paying a convenience premium when you're already pressed. This is exactly how months slide into deficit. Cooking is the move.'

choices.text: Cook with Rohan — split a joint grocery run (₹900 your share) and meal prep together
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Splitting groceries AND cooking together? That's half the cost for the same meals. Rohan is basically a financial asset at this point.'

nodes.narrative: Medical bill handled. Week 4 — final stretch. You've been tracking expenses and the month is tighter than expected. Your phone data plan runs out 3 days before month-end. Options: basic top-up ₹199 (covers 3 days) or upgrade to ₹399 unlimited (28-day plan).

choices.text: Top up with the ₹199 basic plan — you just need 3 days of internet
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Exactly what you need. Not a rupee more. This is the discipline that separates tight months from deficit months.'

choices.text: Buy the ₹399 unlimited plan — it's only ₹200 more and lasts a full month
choices.feedback: Chip: '"It's only ₹200 more" — that phrase has destroyed more budgets than inflation. But okay, if the extra data genuinely helps with work, it's defensible.'

nodes.narrative: Borrowed ₹1,300 from Rohan. Week 4: phone data needs topping up. AND Rohan casually mentions the ₹1,300. He's not pressuring you, but you both know it's there.

choices.text: Repay Rohan immediately (₹1,300) plus basic phone top-up (₹199)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Debt repaid. Clean slate. This is integrity — and it's worth more than ₹1,300 to your friendship. Well done.'

choices.text: Repay Rohan next month, just top up phone for now (₹199)
choices.feedback: Chip sighs. 'You have the money. Pay it back. Rolling informal debt is how friendships quietly break. Don't let ₹1,300 become a wall between you two.'

choices.text: Repay ₹700 now (half), promise the rest by next week, plus phone top-up (₹199)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Partial repayment shows good faith. Not ideal, but better than ignoring it completely. Clear the rest as soon as next month's salary hits.'

nodes.narrative: Month is stretched thin. Final week: you spot a one-day freelance gig — helping a friend's startup with data entry. Pays ₹1,500 for Sunday work. Doesn't conflict with your main job.
nodes.timeSkip: Week 4 - the Sunday before month end...

choices.text: Take the freelance gig (+₹1,500 earned)
choices.feedback: Chip pumps his fist. 'Extra income! Spend less OR earn more — you just pulled the second lever. This changes the end-of-month math completely.'

choices.text: Skip it — you need Sunday to rest and recharge
choices.feedback: Chip nods slowly. 'Rest is valid, especially if burnout is a risk. Just know the month ends with less cushion. Health is wealth too, literally.'

choices.text: Take the gig AND ask if there's more work next weekend (+₹1,500 now, potential future income)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Side income AND networking for more? That's not just earning, that's building an income stream. Future you is taking notes.'

nodes.narrative: Looking decent. Week 4: Rohan wants to do a Swiggy order because you're both exhausted. 'Let's just split one big order, ₹600 each.' You have groceries at home though.

choices.text: Order Swiggy with Rohan (₹600) — you deserve one treat this month
choices.feedback: Chip: 'One Swiggy order is fine. You budgeted for some wants and this qualifies. Enjoy it without guilt.'

choices.text: Cook together with what you have — offer to make dinner (₹0 extra)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Cooked together, saved ₹600, and honestly home food on a Friday is underrated. That's a budget win AND a flatmate bonding moment.'

choices.text: Compromise: cook at home but order one dessert to share (₹150 each)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Home-cooked meal with a Swiggy dessert chaser? ₹150 instead of ₹600 and you still get that delivery dopamine hit. Clever.'

nodes.narrative: Nandi Hills was beautiful, but expensive timing. Final week: you're dangerously low. Need groceries for 5 more days. Every rupee counts now.

choices.text: Buy bare essentials only — dal, rice, eggs, veggies (₹700)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Survival shopping. Not glamorous but it gets you through the week. You made it — barely.'

choices.text: Ask Rohan to split a bulk grocery run and cook together all week (₹450 your share)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Splitting costs with your flatmate is underrated. Same food, lower per-person cost. Teamwork saves the month.'

choices.text: Pick up a quick freelance data-entry gig online over the weekend (+₹1,000) and buy proper groceries (₹900)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Hustle mode activated. You earned extra AND ate properly. Two levers in personal finance: spend less or earn more. You just pulled both. Respect.'

nodes.narrative: Skipped the trip. Smart call financially. Week 4: Rohan feels bad you missed Nandi Hills. He suggests ordering pizza tonight to make up for it. ₹450 your share.

choices.text: Order pizza (₹450) — a small win you actually earned by skipping the trip
choices.feedback: Chip smiles. 'You skipped a ₹1,800 trip and spent ₹450 on pizza. Net savings: ₹1,350. That's a budget win any way you slice it (pun intended).'

choices.text: Cook together instead — save even the ₹450
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Maximum savings, zero regret. You've absolutely nailed this month from a numbers perspective.'

choices.text: Suggest making pizza at home from scratch — flour, sauce, cheese (₹200 total for both of you, your share ₹100)
choices.feedback: Chip: 'Homemade pizza night! Cheaper than delivery, way more fun, and you learned a life skill. Honestly the best option here.'

nodes.narrative: Month end. Your next salary arrives tomorrow. You open your account and do the final tally. Whatever's left from ₹30,000 after all your spending — that's your Month One savings.

nodes.narrative: Month end. Slim margins. You made it through with essentials covered, but the savings number is small — or zero.
nodes.endingNarrative: You survived Month One, barely. Rent paid, food covered, no serious debt. But there's almost nothing left. One more unexpected expense and you'd have been in deficit. This month showed you exactly where the leaks are.
nodes.endingChipQuote: Chip's honest take: You made it out. That counts. But surviving is not the same as thriving. In Month Two, pick just one or two things to do differently — cooking more, skipping one trip. Small changes, big difference.

content.scenario: It's raining and you're running late for college. The metro station is a 10-minute walk. An auto-rickshaw is right outside your building, asking for 150 rupees. The metro would cost 30 rupees but you'll get wet and might be 15 minutes late.
content.prompt: What's the smartest financial move here?

options.text: Always take the auto, time is more valuable than money
Check if this is a one-time thing or a daily habit, one auto ride is fine but daily ones add up to 3,600/month
Walk in the rain to save every rupee
Skip college entirely to avoid the expense

content.explanation: One auto ride in the rain is a reasonable expense. But if you take one every day, that's 150 x 24 working days = 3,600 a month versus 30 x 24 = 720 for the metro. The difference of 2,880 per month is almost enough for your emergency fund. The key is knowing when it's a one-time convenience versus a daily habit eating your budget.

content.scenario: Your friend group of 6 goes out for dinner. You ordered a dosa for 180 rupees. Your friends ordered starters, mains, and desserts. The total bill is 6,600 and someone says 'let's just split equally, that's 1,100 each.'

options.text: Pay the 1,100 to avoid being 'that person'
Politely say you'd prefer to pay for what you ordered, or suggest splitting more fairly
Never go out with friends again to avoid this situation
Order expensive items next time to 'make up for it'

content.explanation: Paying 1,100 for a 180-rupee dosa is a 920-rupee social tax. It's completely okay to politely suggest paying for what you ordered. Most friends will respect it. If they don't, that's useful information too. Being honest about money with friends is a skill that saves you thousands over a year.

content.scenario: You check your bank statement and notice these monthly subscriptions: Netflix 199, Spotify 119, Amazon Prime 149, YouTube Premium 129, a gym you haven't visited in 2 months 999. Total: 1,595 per month.
content.prompt: What's the best approach to handle this?

options.text: Cancel everything, subscriptions are a waste
Keep everything, it's only 1,595 per month
Cancel the ones you don't actively use (especially the gym) and keep 1-2 you actually value
Switch to annual plans for all of them to save a little

content.explanation: The gym alone is 999 rupees for something you're not using. That's 11,988 a year going nowhere. Cancel it, and restart only when you actually go regularly. For OTT, pick 1-2 you genuinely watch and rotate the others. The goal isn't zero subscriptions, it's paying only for what you actually use. Even saving 1,000 a month here means 12,000 a year back in your pocket.
